content: The document outlines a comprehensive framework and assessment tool designed to facilitate the engagement of all relevant healthcare providers in the management of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) at the country level. 1. Public-Private Mix for Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis Management The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a situation assessment tool to support countries in engaging all relevant care providers in the management of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). This tool is part of a broader framework aimed at achieving universal access to quality diagnosis and treatment for all TB cases, including DR-TB. The tool emphasizes the importance of collaboration between public and private healthcare sectors to address the challenges posed by DR-TB. 2. Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (DR-TB) Overview DR-TB includes multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), which is resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin (the two most effective first-line TB drugs), extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), and other forms of drug-resistant TB. In 2013, an estimated 480,000 people developed MDR-TB, and at least 210,000 deaths were attributed to TB globally. Despite advancements in detection, treatment capacity has not kept pace. For example, in 2013, only about 97,000 eligible patients were started on MDR-TB treatment, leaving a significant gap in care. 3. Challenges in DR-TB Management The treatment success rate for MDR-TB remains low at 48% globally, even with the use of second-line TB drugs (SLDs). National TB programs (NTPs) and their partners recognize the critical need for universal access to DR-TB management, but progress has been slow. Efforts to scale up DR-TB management require strategic planning, data-driven decision-making, and the inclusion of all healthcare providers, including those outside the NTP. 4. Public-Private Mix (PPM) in TB Care The PPM approach involves partnerships between public and private healthcare providers to enhance TB care delivery. This includes public-public, public-private, and private-private collaborations. Examples of private sector participants include private hospitals, academic institutions, corporate healthcare providers, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs). The tool highlights the need for NTPs to engage private sector providers while maintaining their leadership role in TB care. 5. Assessment Tool Objectives The primary goal of the assessment tool is to assist countries in evaluating their current PPM activities for TB and DR-TB care. Specific objectives include: Collecting information on existing PPM activities and programmatic management of DR-TB (PMDT), with a focus on non-NTP healthcare providers. Identifying steps to initiate or expand PPM for DR-TB care, ensuring the involvement of all appropriate healthcare providers. 6. Structure of the Assessment Tool The tool is structured as a questionnaire to guide data collection and analysis. It consists of five parts: Part A: Overview of the TB epidemiological situation and NTP performance. Part B: PPM for drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB). Part C: Programmatic management of DR-TB (PMDT). Part D: PPM for DR-TB. Part E: Summary and conclusions. 7. Data Collection and Interpretation The tool provides guidance on the type of data to collect, including both quantitative and qualitative information. It encourages the use of expert opinions and other sources when quantitative data is unavailable. The aim is to produce actionable insights that inform the establishment or expansion of PPM for DR-TB care. 8. Key Considerations for DR-TB Management The extent and quality of DR-TB diagnosis and treatment by non-NTP providers are largely unknown in many countries. NTPs must involve private sector providers and other non-NTP entities in DR-TB management while maintaining oversight and coordination. Strategic expansion of DR-TB management should be guided by carefully collected data and information. 9. Policy and Practice in TB Drug Availability The tool examines policies and practices related to the availability of first-line TB drugs (FLDs) in the private sector. It assesses whether FLDs can be purchased in pharmacies, whether prescriptions are required, and whether there have been stockouts in the past five years. It also evaluates the quality assurance of locally produced TB drugs. 10. TB-HIV Collaborative Activities The tool addresses the integration of TB and HIV care, including policies for HIV testing among TB patients, the proportion of TB patients tested for HIV, and the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV-positive TB patients. 11. Private Sector Engagement The tool assesses the presence and role of the private health sector in TB care, particularly in areas with low public service outreach. It evaluates the proportion of presumptive TB cases that first seek care from private providers and the availability of TB drugs in the private sector. 12. Existing Links Between NTPs and Private Providers The tool examines existing collaborations between NTPs and private TB care providers. It identifies strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) in public-private collaboration and suggests potential private providers that could become partners in DR-TB care. 13. Strategic Planning for DR-TB Management The tool emphasizes the importance of standardized monitoring using consistent indicators that are acceptable to countries and implementing partners. It calls for a bold and concerted effort to address DR-TB care comprehensively, with a focus on engaging all healthcare providers. This detailed explanation provides a clear understanding of the document's content, emphasizing the importance of a collaborative approach to managing drug-resistant tuberculosis.
